newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE-Cheeseburgers latest focus in Israel's dietary debates.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Cheeseburgers latest focus in Israel's dietary debates.

text.p: McDonald's golden arches are the latest lightning rod in the fight for the soul -- and stomach -- of Israel, a country long racked by debates over biblical injunctions on diet.
Many religious Israelis say that advertisements for McDonald's cheeseburgers, which break kosher dietary laws by mixing meat and dairy products, have no place on Jewish television sets.

"Religious parties are entering into your plate," carped McDonald's Israel managing director Omri Padan, fingering a statuette of Ronald McDonald, the clown mascot of the multinational fast-food powerhouse.
"They asked us to remove these cheeseburger advertisements from the TV. They claim it's hurting the public feeling to see meat and cheese together," Padan told Reuters.
Indeed, National Religious Party lawmaker Avner Shaki has led a crusade against television advertising of the Mac Royale cheeseburger -- the metric world's version of the U.S. "Quarter Pounder."
ADS CAUSE OFFENCE

"When you advertise non-kosher foods it's like you give it to people to eat. You would like them to come and eat in this restaurant. It's causing us harm psychologically. It's offending us," Shaki told Reuters.
Padan, who counts seven cheese-free kosher franchises among the 36 McDonald's restaurants in Israel, bristled at the idea that religious "food police" would set his advertising policy.
"This is exactly Khomeinism in Israel," Padan said, referring to the late Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, leader of Iran's 1979 Islamic revolution.
"It is telling the business community...that somebody will dictate on a religious basis what to advertise and what not.
"If these religious parties will continue to impose new laws and new restrictions on the business community, Israel will look more and more similar to Iran," Padan said.
But for Shaki, democracy in the Jewish state entails protection of the rights of religious Jews not to watch advertisements they consider profane.
"More than 70 percent of the Jewish population in Israel observe kosher food laws. They are opposed to cheeseburgers."
HALF CHOOSE CHEESEBURGERS
Padan sees the numbers differently.
"More than 50 percent prefer to buy a hamburger with cheese...it's the most successful hamburger we have in Israel."
The cheeseburger controversy had Israel Television's Channel Two in a pickle.
Station director Nachman Shai said hundreds of complaints had prompted a survey of public views towards the sandwich.
"More or less, the Israeli public is divided when it comes to this famous cheeseburger commercial," Shai told Reuters.

"Many people that are not necessarily Orthodox or even religious did not simply like the idea of a cheeseburger on Israeli television," Shai said, adding that he himself indulged in the occasional cheeseburger and milkshake.
He said the television had to ensure that specific groups in the public would not be offended by commercials and programming and would decide on the advertisement's fate.
"Only once in Channel Two's history did we decide to block a commercial. It went to the supreme court and we lost," he said.
Padan said he welcomed a court battle.

"This has nothing to do with McDonald's international against the religious group in Israel. We have an Israeli problem here of freedom of choice, freedom of work, freedom of speech, freedom of advertisement."
